title: Thermal Conduction in Solids
short_intro: Thermal conduction is the process of heat transfer through a material medium from regions of higher temperature to regions of lower temperature without the actual bulk movement of the medium particles. It is the primary mode of heat transfer in opaque solids, governed by temperature gradients and the microscopic interactions of lattice vibrations and free electrons.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Definition of thermal conductivity, Searle's and Ingen-Hausz methods, steady state heat flow, linear flow of heat through slabs and composite bars.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Wiedemann-Franz law, temperature dependence of thermal conductivity, thermal diffusivity, radial heat flow in cylinders and spheres, phonon scattering mechanisms in non-metals.

prerequisites: Concept of Temperature and Zeroth Law
Kinetic theory of gases and microscopic interpretation of temperature

concept_notes.heading: Mechanism of Thermal Conduction
bullets: In non-metals and insulators, thermal conduction occurs primarily via the propagation of elastic waves or lattice vibrations known as phonons.
In metals, thermal conduction is dominated by the diffusion of free conduction electrons which transport both charge and kinetic energy effectively.
The steady state is achieved when the temperature at every point within the conductor remains constant with respect to time, meaning no further heat is absorbed by any cross-section.

concept_notes.heading: Coefficient of Thermal Conductivity
bullets: Thermal conductivity (K) is a material property that quantifies its ability to conduct heat.
The rate of heat flow is directly proportional to the cross-sectional area and the temperature gradient, and inversely proportional to the length of the conductor.
SI units of thermal conductivity are W m<sup>-1</sup> K<sup>-1</sup> or J s<sup>-1<sup> m<sup>-1</sup> K<sup>-1</sup>.

concept_notes.heading: Thermal Resistance and Composite Slabs
bullets: Thermal resistance is defined as the ratio of temperature difference to the rate of heat flow, analogous to electrical resistance.
For bodies in series, the equivalent thermal resistance is the sum of individual thermal resistances: R<sub>eq</sub> = R<sub>1</sub> + R<sub>2</sub>.
For bodies in parallel, the reciprocal of the equivalent thermal resistance is the sum of reciprocals of individual thermal resistances.

concept_notes.heading: Wiedemann-Franz Law
bullets: The law states that the ratio of the thermal conductivity (K) to the electrical conductivity (σ) of a metal is directly proportional to the absolute temperature (T).
The proportionality constant is known as the Lorenz number (L), which is approximately independent of the specific metal at moderate to high temperatures.
Expressed mathematically as K / (σ T) = L, where L ≈ 2.44 × 10<sup>-8</sup> V<sup>2</sup> K<sup>-2</sup>.

derivations.title: Fourier's Law of Heat Conduction and Temperature Gradient
derivations.conditions: Steady state heat flow through a uniform slab of cross-sectional area A and thickness x.
steps: Assume a uniform slab of thickness dx with temperature difference dT across it.
The rate of heat flow dQ/dt is experimentally found to be proportional to area A and temperature gradient -dT/dx.
Introduce the proportionality constant K (thermal conductivity): dQ/dt = -K A (dT/dx).
Integrate across a finite length L with temperatures T1 and T2 to obtain total heat transfer.

derivations.title: Equivalent Thermal Resistance for Composite Slabs in Series
derivations.conditions: Two slabs of thicknesses L1, L2, thermal conductivities K1, K2, and identical cross-sectional area A placed in series.
steps: Let the temperatures at the outer faces be T1 and T3, and at the junction be T2.
In steady state, the rate of heat flow through both slabs must be equal: H = H1 = H2.
Write the heat flow equations for each slab: H = \frac{KA(T_1 - T_2)}{L_1} and H = \frac{K_2A(T_2 - T_3)}{L_2}.
Express temperature drops as T1 - T2 = H(L1 / K1A) and T2 - T3 = H(L2 / K2A).
Add the equations to eliminate T2, yielding H = \frac{T_1 - T_3}{(L_1/K_1A) + (L_2/K_2A)}.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Temperature Profile along a Uniform Conductor in Steady State
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A linear graph of temperature (T) on the y-axis versus distance from the hot end (x) on the x-axis, showing a constant negative slope.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: The constant slope indicates a uniform temperature gradient (dT/dx = constant) throughout the length of the conductor in steady state.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Tested in conceptual multiple-choice questions to differentiate between steady state and variable state temperature profiles.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Searle's Apparatus Experiment
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Schematic setup showing a metal rod heated at one end by steam and cooled at the other by a continuous water flow, with thermometers at fixed intervals.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Used to determine the absolute thermal conductivity of a good conductor by measuring steady-state temperatures and mass flow rate of cooling water.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Direct questions on experimental formulas and precautions for measuring K.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Ingen-Hausz Experiment
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Several rods of different materials of identical dimensions coated with wax, dipped at one end into a hot water bath.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: The length to which wax melts on each rod is proportional to the square root of its thermal conductivity.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Comparative questions on thermal conductivities using the relation l^2 ∝ K.

solved_numericals.question: A brass rod of length 0.5 m and cross-sectional area 2 cm<sup>2</sup> has its ends maintained at 100°C and 0°C. If the thermal conductivity of brass is 109 W m<sup>-1</sup> K<sup>-1</sup>, calculate the rate of heat flow through the rod in steady state.
solution_steps: Identify given values: L = 0.5 m, A = 2 cm<sup>2</sup> = 2 × 10<sup>-4</sup> m<sup>2</sup>, T1 = 100°C, T2 = 0°C, K = 109 W m<sup>-1</sup> K<sup>-1</sup>.
Apply Fourier's law formula: H = \frac{KA(T_1 - T_2)}{L}.

solved_numericals.question: Two identical metal rods are connected in series. Their thermal conductivities are K1 = 200 W m<sup>-1</sup> K<sup>-1</sup> and K2 = 400 W m<sup>-1</sup> K<sup>-1</sup>. If the free ends are kept at 100°C and 0°C respectively, find the temperature of the junction in steady state.
solution_steps: Let the length of each rod be L and cross-sectional area be A. Let junction temperature be T.
In steady state, the rate of heat flow through both rods is equal: H1 = H2.
Set up the equation: \frac{K_1 A (100 - T)}{L} = \frac{K_2 A (T - 0)}{L}.
Cancel common terms A and L, and substitute K1 and K2: 200(100 - T) = 400(T).

solved_numericals.question: Using the Wiedemann-Franz law, calculate the theoretical thermal conductivity of a metal at 300 K if its electrical conductivity is 6 × 10<sup>7</sup> Ω<sup>-1</sup> m<sup>-1</sup> and the Lorenz number is 2.45 × 10<sup>-8</sup> V<sup>2</sup> K<sup>-2</sup>.
solution_steps: Identify given values: T = 300 K, σ = 6 × 10<sup>7</sup> Ω<sup>-1</sup> m<sup>-1</sup>, L = 2.45 × 10<sup>-8</sup> V<sup>2</sup> K<sup>-2</sup>.
Recall Wiedemann-Franz relation: K = L σ T.
Calculate product: K = 2.45 × 6 × 300 × 10<sup>-1</sup> = 4410 × 0.1 = 441 W m<sup>-1</sup> K<sup>-1</sup>.

assumptions_and_limitations: Fourier's law assumes that thermal conductivity K is independent of temperature, which is strictly valid only for small temperature intervals.
Heat flow equations assume steady state conditions where internal energy of the conductor elements does not change with time.
Lateral heat losses to the surrounding medium are neglected in standard 1D linear conduction models.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Heat flows faster in a conductor if its temperature is higher, regardless of temperature gradient.
common_misconceptions.correct: Heat flow rate depends strictly on the temperature gradient (dT/dx) and thermal conductivity, not the absolute temperature alone.
common_misconceptions.why: Fourier's law dictates that heat current is driven by spatial temperature differences, not absolute thermal levels.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Thermal conductivity and heat capacity are the same physical property.
common_misconceptions.correct: Thermal conductivity measures the rate of heat transport, whereas heat capacity measures the ability to store thermal energy.
common_misconceptions.why: They govern different aspects of thermal behavior; their ratio determines thermal diffusivity.

quick_revision: Thermal conductivity K measures a material's intrinsic ability to conduct heat via electrons and phonons.
In steady state, the temperature gradient along a uniform rod is constant.
Thermal resistance in series adds algebraically, analogous to electrical resistors.
Wiedemann-Franz law links thermal and electrical conductivities through the Lorenz number proportional to temperature.
